the groundwater arsenic in the Red River plain aquifers is released from Fe-oxided minerals by the reduction of Fe-oxides by organic carbon, and that the release is delayed by sorption onto aquifer material and that the release and sorption are controlled by the kinetics and thermodynamics of the organic carbon degradation.

the groundwater arsenic in the Red River floodplain decreases with increasing aquifer age due to the combined effects of (1) a decrease in the reactivity of the organic carbon, (2) the reduction of Fe-oxides and the associated release of As and Fe(II) into the groundwater, (3) the precipitation of siderite and the associated release and consumption of protons, and (4) the associated dissolution of carbonate minerals and the associated buffering capacity of the aquifer.

how the arsenic content of groundwater evolves over a 600,000 year period in an aquifer that has been contaminated with arsenic containing Fe-oxide.

the arsenic content in the groundwater of the Red River floodplain aquifers is a function of the burial age of the aquifer and the organic carbon content of the sediment.
the arsenic concentration in the groundwater is controlled by the kinetics of organic degradation and the reactivity of Fe-oxides.
the arsenic content of the groundwater is controlled by the kinetics of organic material degradation and the kinetics of Fe(oxide)-reduction.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a combination of a high organic carbon content, a high reactivity of Fe-oxides and a low number of sorption site, together with a high buffering capacity, leads to a high groundwater arsenic content.

the arsenic content of the groundwater decreases with age because of the decrease in the number of sorbed arsenic ions and the decrease in the amount of arsenic released from Fe-oxide, which is controlled by the decrease in the Fe-oxide reactivity.
the groundwater arsenic is controlled by the kinetics of organic degradation and Fe-oxide redox reactions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution in the groundwater arsenics content over a long time scale is controlled by both the kinetics of organic degradation and the kinetics of Fe(II) oxidation.

the arsenic content in groundwater is not only determined by the reactivity of Fe-oxides and organic carbon, but also by the kinetics and thermodynamics of carbonate precipitation and dissolution and the kinetics of sorption of arsenate onto sediment.

the arsenic content of groundwater is controlled by a combination of processes and that it is not possible to explain the arsenic concentration in groundwater solely in terms of the reactivity of the arsenic bearing minerals or by the presence of organic carbon.
